title: Fourier Analysis and Representation of Square Waves
short_intro: A square wave is a periodic waveform that alternates instantaneously between two distinct fixed levels at regular intervals. Its frequency spectrum contains only fundamental frequency and odd harmonic components with amplitudes inversely proportional to the harmonic number.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the definition of periodic functions, time period, frequency, and basic identification of wave components.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed Fourier series expansion of square waves, evaluation of Fourier coefficients (a<sub>0</sub>, a<sub>n</sub>, b<sub>n</sub>), root-mean-square (RMS) value, energy distribution, and Gibbs phenomenon.

prerequisites: Integration techniques for definite integrals (Euler-Fourier formulas)
Concept of harmonics and fundamental frequency in wave motion

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Symmetry Properties
bullets: A symmetric square wave alternates between values -V and +V with a total time period T.
Due to its time-reversal antisymmetry about the origin f(-t) = -f(t), the square wave is an odd function.
Because it is an odd function, all cosine coefficients (a<sub>n</sub>) in its Fourier series expansion vanish identically, leaving only sine terms.

concept_notes.heading: Frequency Spectrum and Harmonics
bullets: The Fourier expansion of a square wave consists exclusively of the fundamental frequency and its odd harmonics: 3ω, 5ω, 7ω, etc.
Even harmonics are completely absent due to half-wave antisymmetry: f(t + T/2) = -f(t).
The amplitude of the n-th harmonic is inversely proportional to n, falling off as 1/n.

concept_notes.heading: Power and RMS Value
bullets: The root-mean-square (RMS) value of a symmetric square wave oscillating between -V and +V is simply V.
Parseval's theorem relates the total average power of the square wave to the sum of the powers contained in its individual harmonic components.
Higher-order harmonics contribute progressively less to the total signal energy.

concept_notes.heading: Gibbs Phenomenon
bullets: When a square wave is reconstructed using a finite number of terms in its Fourier series, overshoots and ripples consistently appear near the points of discontinuity.
The overshoot magnitude remains approximately 9% of the step height regardless of how many terms are added.
This non-uniform convergence behavior at discontinuities is known as the Gibbs phenomenon.

derivations.title: Fourier Series Expansion of a Symmetric Square Wave
derivations.conditions: Square wave defined as f(t) = V for 0 < t < T/2 and f(t) = -V for T/2 < t < T
steps: Write the general Fourier series: f(t) = a_0 / 2 + sum_{n=1}^infty [a_n \cos(n\omega t) + b_n \sin(n\omega t)].
Evaluate the average value a_0 = (2/T) \int_0^T f(t) dt = 0 due to wave symmetry.
Evaluate a_n = (2/T) \int_0^T f(t) \cos(n\omega t) dt = 0 because f(t) is an odd function multiplied by an even function.
Evaluate b_n = (2/T) \int_0^T f(t) \sin(n\omega t) dt = \frac{4V}{n\pi} for odd n, and 0 for even n.

derivations.title: RMS Value of a Square Wave
steps: Write the definition of RMS value: V_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T [f(t)]^2 dt}.
Substitute the squared function [f(t)]^2 = V^2 over the entire period T.
Perform the integration: V_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \left[ V^2 \frac{T}{2} + V^2 \frac{T}{2} \right]} = \sqrt{V^2}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Time-Domain Square Waveform
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of amplitude f(t) on the y-axis versus time t on the x-axis, showing instantaneous transitions between +V and -V at intervals of T/2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the rectangular pulses repeating every period T with sharp vertical edges representing infinite slope discontinuities.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification questions and determining time period and peak voltage.

solved_numericals.question: A symmetric square wave has a peak voltage of 10 V. What is the root-mean-square (RMS) value of this voltage?
solution_steps: Recall the formula for the RMS value of a symmetric square wave: V_{rms} = V.
Identify the given peak voltage V = 10 V.

solved_numericals.question: Find the amplitude of the third harmonic component in the Fourier series expansion of a square wave whose peak amplitude is 5 V.
solution_steps: The general amplitude formula for the n-th harmonic of a square wave is A_n = \frac{4V}{n\pi}.
Substitute V = 5 V and n = 3 into the formula.

solved_numericals.question: A square wave of peak amplitude V and frequency 50 Hz is passed through an ideal low-pass filter that cuts off all frequencies above 120 Hz. Which harmonic frequencies are allowed to pass through the filter?
solution_steps: The fundamental frequency is f_1 = 50 Hz.
The square wave contains odd harmonics: f_1 = 50 Hz, f_3 = 150 Hz, f_5 = 250 Hz, etc.
The low-pass filter cutoff is 120 Hz, meaning only frequencies less than or equal to 120 Hz pass.
Therefore, only the fundamental frequency (50 Hz) passes through, as the 3rd harmonic (150 Hz) exceeds the cutoff.

assumptions_and_limitations: Transitions between voltage levels are assumed to be instantaneous (zero rise time and fall time), which is physically impossible in real electronic circuits due to stray capacitances and inductances.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A square wave contains both even and odd harmonics.
common_misconceptions.correct: A symmetric square wave contains only odd harmonics.
common_misconceptions.why: Half-wave antisymmetry eliminates all even harmonic coefficients in the Fourier expansion.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The RMS value of a square wave is equal to its peak value divided by square root of 2.
common_misconceptions.correct: The RMS value of a symmetric square wave is exactly equal to its peak value (V).
common_misconceptions.why: Since the square wave spends 100% of its time at magnitude V (either +V or -V), the time average of V^2 is V^2, making V_{rms} = V.

quick_revision: Square waves consist of fundamental and odd harmonics with amplitudes proportional to 1/n.
Fourier Series of Symmetric Square Wave: f(t) = \frac{4V}{\pi} \left( \sin(\omega t) + \frac{1}{3}\sin(3\omega t) + \frac{1}{5}\sin(5\omega t) + \dots \right)
Fourier Coefficient b_n: b_n = \begin{cases} \frac{4V}{n\pi} & \text{for } n = 1, 3, 5, \dots \\ 0 & \text{for } n = 2, 4, 6, \dots \end{cases}
